```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
set.seed(313)

# Causal graphs: letters in circles, one panel per value of `panel`. A circle's size is
# fixed on the page, in inches, while the figure's size decides how many inches a data
# unit is. draw_dag measures both on the graphics device open when it is called, and
# stops every arrow `gap` inches short of the circles.
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  dot <- 10; stroke <- 0.5; lw <- 0.5
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = 4.5) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void()
  # inches per data unit: the panels share what the strips and spacing leave of the figure
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  # R draws a circle of radius 0.375 times its font size (shape 21); outline included
  r <- 0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 + stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |> rename(x0 = x, y0 = y) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(len = sqrt((x - x0)^2 + (y - y0)^2), ux = (x - x0) / len, uy = (y - y0) / len,
           # the end also clears half the line width, which the rounded tip adds
           s0 = (r + gap) / per_unit, s1 = (r + gap + lw * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = lw)
}
```

## In class

1. A game, then a discussion of it.
2. A discussion of the arguments you brought.
3. Problems 1 and 2, by hand.
4. A discussion of a model that makes decisions about people.
5. A debate, then a vote.

Discussions 1 to 3 are in groups of three or four, then with the room.
For discussion 4 the room splits into four parts. Each problem is gone
through as soon as the room has tried it. Everything under "Optional,
can be done at home" is practice for afterward.

## Discussion 1: absurd trolley problems

In your group, open
[Absurd Trolley Problems](https://neal.fun/absurd-trolley-problems/)
on one device and play for about six minutes, choosing together. Note
the scenarios where the group disagreed, and the ones you personally
found hard to choose.

1. Take one scenario where the group disagreed. Which framework was
   each side using?
2. Did any of your choices depend on a prediction of what would happen?
   How sure of it were you?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Frameworks on the track" collapse="true"}
In the original problem, pulling the lever to save five people at the
cost of one is what a consequentialist who counts lives would do.
Refusing to pull it, because diverting the trolley makes you the cause
of one death while doing nothing lets five die, is one deontological
answer: it rests on a difference between doing and allowing. Other
deontologists allow pulling the lever, by the doctrine of double
effect: the one death is foreseen but not intended. A virtue ethicist
asks what a good person would do there, and can answer either way. Where a choice turned on a prediction, the consequentialist's
answer depended on a causal claim, and the game gives no way to check
it.
:::

## Discussion 2: the arguments you brought

Put your arguments side by side and choose one.

1. What is the action, and which outcome does the argument count?
   Whose good is counted, and whose is left out?
2. Draw the causal graph the argument needs, with an arrow for each
   cause-and-effect claim you listed. Mark the action.
3. Try to draw a second graph that fits the same evidence and under
   which the action does nothing. If the evidence makes every such
   graph hard to believe, say what in the evidence does that.
4. Argue against the policy without disputing any of its causal
   claims. Which framework are you using?

Each group's graph, and its argument from question 4, go on the screen.

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Rival graphs" collapse="true"}
Most arguments have a rival graph of one of two kinds: a common cause
of the action and the outcome, or an arrow that points the other way.
A rival graph does not show that your argument is wrong. It shows what
evidence would tell the two graphs apart, which is usually a comparison
in which the action was not chosen by the people, or the places, that
also determine the outcome. If the argument rests on a randomized
trial, no common cause of the assignment and the outcome can explain
its result, because a coin decided who was assigned the action. What
is left to question includes chance, whether what the coin assigned is
the action the argument is about (some people do not take what they
are assigned), and whether the people in the trial are like the people
the policy is for.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Accepting the causal claims" collapse="true"}
A utilitarian who accepts every causal claim can still object that the
outcome counted is not the good that matters, or that the count leaves
out people the policy affects. A deontologist can object that the
policy breaks a rule, such as consent, whatever its effects. A virtue
ethicist can object that it expresses a vice, such as indifference to
the people it harms. These are disagreements about what matters, and
better evidence for the causal claims does not settle them.
:::

## Problems

Before you start, from memory: what does the adjustment formula
average, and with what weights?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
It averages the outcome among people with $X = x$ within each value of
$Z$, with weights $P(Z = z)$: how common each value of $Z$ is in the
whole population, not among the people with $X = x$.
:::

### 1. Conditioning and intervening

A program in the style of the reading's. $U_1, \dots, U_5$ are
independent, with $U_1 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(0.5)$, $U_2 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(0.6)$,
$U_3 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(0.2)$, $U_4 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(0.4)$ and
$U_5 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(0.1)$, where $\mathrm{Ber}(0.6)$ is 1 with
probability 0.6 and 0 otherwise.

1. $X := U_1$ (exercise)
2. $W :=$ if $X = 1$ then $U_3$ else $U_2$ (overweight)
3. $H :=$ if $X = 1$ then $U_5$ else $U_4$ (heart disease)

(a) Draw the graph.

(b) Compute $P(W = 1)$ and $P(X = 0 \mid W = 1)$.

(c) Compute $P(H = 1)$, $P(H = 1 \mid W = 1)$ and $P(H = 1 \mid W = 0)$.

(d) A program changes everyone's weight to normal: $W := 0$. Compute
$P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 0))$. What does the program do to heart disease?

(e) Compute the average treatment effect of exercise on heart disease,
and compare it with $P(H = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(H = 1 \mid X = 0)$. Are
they equal? Why?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (b), use Bayes' rule: $P(X = 0 \mid W = 1) = P(W = 1 \mid X = 0)\,P(X = 0)/P(W = 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (c), condition on $X$ first. Given $X$, $W$ and $H$ come from different coins, so they are independent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 3"}
For (d), replace line 2 by $W := 0$ and keep the other two lines. Which variables does $H$ depend on now?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $W \leftarrow X \to H$, a fork.

(b) $P(W = 1) = 0.5 \times 0.2 + 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.4$, and
$P(X = 0 \mid W = 1) = 0.5 \times 0.6 / 0.4 = 0.75$.

(c) $P(H = 1) = 0.5 \times 0.1 + 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.25$. Given $X$, $H$
does not depend on $W$, so
$P(H = 1 \mid W = 1) = 0.75 \times 0.4 + 0.25 \times 0.1 = 0.325$.
For $W = 0$: $P(W = 0) = 0.6$ and
$P(X = 0 \mid W = 0) = 0.5 \times 0.4/0.6 = 1/3$, so
$P(H = 1 \mid W = 0) = \tfrac13 \times 0.4 + \tfrac23 \times 0.1 = 0.2$.
Overweight people have heart disease at 0.325, the others at 0.2.

(d) The line for $H$ is unchanged and $X$ keeps its distribution, so
$P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 0)) = P(H = 1) = 0.25$, and the same for
$do(W := 1)$. The weight program does nothing to heart disease, although
overweight people had 12.5 points more of it.

(e) $E[H \mid do(X := 1)] - E[H \mid do(X := 0)] = 0.1 - 0.4 = -0.3$,
and $P(H = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(H = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.1 - 0.4 = -0.3$.
They are equal because no arrow points into $X$: it is set by a coin, as
in a randomized trial, so there is no backdoor path from $X$ to $H$.
Overweight people exercise less often (25% of them, against 50% of
everyone), and that is where their extra heart disease comes from.
:::

### 2. Adjusting for a confounder

A school offers a revision app before a test. Students who passed the
previous year's test ($Z = 1$) are more likely to use it ($X = 1$). The
outcome is passing this year ($Y = 1$).

| | used the app ($X = 1$) | did not ($X = 0$) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| passed last year ($Z = 1$), 500 students | 320 of 400 passed (80%) | 70 of 100 passed (70%) |
| did not ($Z = 0$), 500 students | 50 of 100 passed (50%) | 120 of 400 passed (30%) |

(a) Compute the pass rates of users and non-users, and the difference.

(b) Draw the graph you would assume, and compute the average treatment
effect of the app with the adjustment formula.

(c) Compute the difference within each row. How does the average
treatment effect combine the two?

(d) A second school has the same pass rates within each cell of the
table, but only 20% of its students passed last year. What is the
average treatment effect of the app there?

(e) A head teacher asks whether to buy the app for every student. Which
of your numbers would you report, and what would you say about it?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a), count the users who passed in both rows, and divide by all users.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (b), the adjustment formula weights each row by its share of all students, not by its share of users.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Users: $(320 + 50)/500 = 0.74$. Non-users: $(70 + 120)/500 = 0.38$.
The difference is $0.36$.

(b) $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to Y$.
$E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] = 0.8 \times 0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.65$ and
$E[Y \mid do(X := 0)] = 0.7 \times 0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.50$, so the
average treatment effect is $0.15$.

(c) $0.80 - 0.70 = 0.10$ among students who passed last year, and
$0.50 - 0.30 = 0.20$ among those who did not. The average treatment
effect is their average weighted by $P(Z = z)$:
$0.10 \times 0.5 + 0.20 \times 0.5 = 0.15$.

(d) $0.10 \times 0.2 + 0.20 \times 0.8 = 0.18$.

(e) The average treatment effect, 0.15, compares everyone using the app
with nobody using it, in this school's mix of students. The head
teacher's decision is different in two ways. Half the students already
use the app, so the comparison is with today's pass rate,
$560/1000 = 0.56$. If everyone used it the rate would be 0.65, an
increase of 0.09. And buying the app gives access, not use, so the
increase would be smaller if some students did not use it. The effect
among today's non-users is $(100 \times 0.10 + 400 \times 0.20)/500 = 0.18$,
the same as in (d), because the non-users have the second school's mix:
20% of them passed last year. All of it rests on the graph. If something
unmeasured, such as motivation, pushed students both to use the app and
to pass, adjusting for $Z$ would not give the effect.
:::

## Discussion 3: a model that decides about people

Think of a predictive algorithm that makes, or helps to make, decisions
with large effects on people: which applicants get a loan, which
patients a GP sees first, which benefit claims are checked for fraud.
Choose one in your group.

1. Describe the scenario: who uses the model, what it predicts, from
   what data, and what is decided with it.
2. Half the groups take the four Belmont--Menlo principles, and half
   take the five Cs (consent; clarity; consistency and trust; control
   and transparency; consequences). For each one, say what would have
   to be in place: a feature of the system, or a procedure around it.
3. Which of your requirements could be checked only with a causal
   claim?

Two or three groups describe their scenario and its requirements to the
room.

::: {.callout-note .answer title="An example: suggestions for GPs" collapse="true"}
A model suggests treatments to NHS GPs, to help them get through
patient cases faster. It needs private information about each patient,
and may store it. It would need, among other things:

- informed consent from the patient, or from someone legally acting
  for them, to the use and storage of their data, and the data held
  securely or not at all (respect for persons; consent);
- a clear account to the patient of how the model is used, how their
  data is used and what happens to the data afterward (clarity;
  consistency and trust; beneficence);
- no use of the model for a patient who says no (control and
  transparency; beneficence);
- high accuracy, since a wrong suggestion can harm a patient
  (beneficence);
- a model that is demonstrably fair across demographic groups, since
  there are documented cases of medical algorithms biased by race or by
  sex (justice; consistency and trust);
- storage and processing that meet data-protection law such as the
  GDPR (respect for law and the public interest);
- care that its records cannot be combined with other sources to
  identify patients (consequences).

Accuracy is a property of the predictions. Whether patients do better
when their GP uses the suggestions than when the GP does not is an
effect, and that requirement needs a causal claim.
:::

## Discussion 4: the case for one framework

The room splits into four parts. Each part prepares the strongest case
it can for one statement.

1. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on consequentialist ethics.
2. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on deontological ethics.
3. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on virtue ethics.
4. Ethical data science and AI development requires us to lean mostly
   on pragmatic ethics.

Five minutes to prepare, then a minute for each part.
Each case should answer the strongest objection to it. For
consequentialism, one objection is the lecture's last question: does it
become more or less defensible once you have to write the causal model
down?

Then everyone votes, whichever part they argued for. Which account are
you most convinced of: consequentialist, deontological, virtue or
pragmatic ethics, a combination, or none of them?

## If there is time

- "Correlation (more generally, association) is not causation." This
  is true and important, but can it be misused?
- Can causality be useful in the context of reproducibility? In
  designing and communicating studies?
- A company tests two versions of its app on its users, without telling
  them, to see which version keeps them using the app longer. Which of
  the Belmont--Menlo principles does this touch? How would each of the
  four frameworks judge it?
- Find a sentence in a news report of an observational study that
  avoids saying "causes" but implies a cause. What graph does it
  assume?

## To finish

One sentence, individually: what is the difference between
$P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1)$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X := 1))$?

Bring one score or algorithm used to make decisions about people. Write

### 3. Omitted-variable bias

In the linear model of the notes,
$Z := U_Z$, $X := \alpha Z + U_X$, $Y := \beta X + \gamma Z + U_Y$, with
independent mean-zero noise, take $\alpha = 2$, $\gamma = 1$,
$\beta = 0.5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \operatorname{Var}(U_X) = 1$.

(a) Compute $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)$ and the
slope of $Y$ on $X$ alone.

(b) Repeat with $\gamma = -1$.

(c) Repeat with $\gamma = 1$ and $\beta = 0$. What would someone with data
on $X$ and $Y$ alone conclude?

(d) Is the error in (a) a bias or a variance? What happens to it as the
sample grows?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
$Z$ and $U_X$ are independent, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z) + \operatorname{Var}(U_X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4 + 1 = 5$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z) = \alpha \operatorname{Var}(Z) = 2$. The slope
is $\beta + \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X) = 0.5 + 2/5 = 0.9$.

(b) $0.5 - 2/5 = 0.1$: the bias has the sign of $\gamma\alpha$, and here
it almost hides the effect.

(c) $0 + 2/5 = 0.4$. They would see a positive slope and could conclude
that raising $X$ raises $Y$, when intervening on $X$ does nothing.

(d) A bias. The slope converges to $0.9$ as the sample grows: the
estimates concentrate around $0.9$, not around the effect, $0.5$.
:::

### 4. Choosing an adjustment set

```{r five_nodes, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.6, fig.width=5}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "X", "M", "Y", "W"),
                    x = c(1, 0, 1, 2, 2.9), y = c(1.1, 0, -0.3, 0, 1.1)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "X", "M", "X", "W"),
                    to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y", "Y")),
         xlim = c(-0.5, 3.4), ylim = c(-0.6, 1.4))
```

(a) List the backdoor paths from $X$ to $Y$.

(b) Which of these sets satisfy the backdoor criterion: the empty set,
$\{Z\}$, $\{M\}$, $\{Z, M\}$, $\{W\}$, $\{Z, W\}$?

(c) In a linear model, what does the coefficient on $X$ estimate if you
adjust for $\{Z, M\}$?

(d) If more than one of the sets in (b) satisfies the criterion, which
would you use, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
A backdoor path starts with an arrow into $X$. How many arrows point into $X$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) One: $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$.

(b) $\{Z\}$ and $\{Z, W\}$. The empty set and $\{W\}$ leave the back
door open. $\{M\}$ and $\{Z, M\}$ contain a descendant of $X$.

(c) The direct effect of $X$, along the arrow $X \to Y$: the part that
does not go through $M$. It is not the total effect of $X$. (It is the
direct effect because in this graph nothing else affects both $M$ and
$Y$.)

(d) $\{Z\}$ and $\{Z, W\}$ both satisfy it. Use $\{Z, W\}$: $W$ is not
a confounder, so leaving it out causes no bias, but it explains some of
the variation in $Y$, and the estimate that uses it is usually less
variable.
:::

### 5. The graph behind an argument

A university says: "Students who use the library more get better
grades. We will extend the library's opening hours, because using the
library improves grades."

(a) Draw the causal graph the argument presupposes, and mark the action.

(b) Add one variable that would make the observed difference larger
than the effect, with its arrows.

(c) What comparison would support the university's claim?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
The university's evidence compares students. Its action changes opening hours. Are those the same thing?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Opening hours (the action) $\to$ library use $\to$ grades. The
argument needs the arrow from library use to grades, and an arrow from
opening hours to library use.

(b) For example motivation, or how well a student was already doing,
with arrows into library use and into grades. If it raises both, the
students who use the library more would have had better grades anyway,
so the observed difference is larger than the effect.

(c) Grades before and after the hours were extended, against a
comparable university or set of courses where they were not; or terms,
or sites, chosen at random to have longer hours. The comparison of
students who use the library more with those who use it less answers a
question about those students.
:::

### 6. Prediction letters and reinforcement-learning letters

The decision whether to prescribe hormone therapy to prevent heart
disease can be written with the letters used for prediction or with
those of reinforcement learning.

(a) Write it with the letters used for prediction. Say what the
treatment, the outcome and a confounder are, and write the quantity a
doctor needs with $do(\cdot)$.

(b) Write it with the letters of reinforcement learning, with the
one-line declaration at the top. Say what the state, the action, the
reward, the policy and the utility are.

(c) Which letters would mean different things if you used them in both
answers?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a), what does the doctor choose, and what could affect both that choice and heart disease? For (b), what does the doctor know when choosing?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $X = 1$ if the doctor prescribes hormone therapy, $Y = 1$ if the
woman has coronary heart disease within five years, $Z$ her
socioeconomic status.
A doctor needs $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X := 1))$ against
$P(Y = 1 \mid do(X := 0))$, not $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1)$ against
$P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0)$.

(b) **Notation:** this answer uses the letters of reinforcement
learning, $S$ state, $A$ action, $R$ reward, $\pi$ policy, $U$ utility. $S$ is
the patient's state: age, time since the menopause, risk factors. $A$ is
prescribe or do not. $\pi$ is the prescribing rule from state to
action. $R$ is a measured reward, such as no heart attack recorded in
five years. $U$ is what we care about: her health, including breast
cancer, stroke and fractures as well as the heart.

(c) $A$, $R$ and $U$. With the letters used for prediction they are a
sensitive attribute, a risk score and an unobserved variable.
:::

### 7. Hormone therapy

The notes' section on hormone therapy and heart disease gives the three
studies.

(a) The 1996 estimate (0.39) and the 2008 estimates (1.42 over the first
two years, 0.96 over the whole follow-up) come from the same cohort.
Which comparison did each make?

(b) Draw a graph under which the 1996 estimate is confounded.

(c) Which comparison matches the decision a doctor makes, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a), ask which two groups each analysis compares.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) 1996: women who took estrogen with progestin against women who did
not use hormones, adjusted for measured confounders. 2008: women who
started against women who did not start, both followed from the same
point, analyzed as the trial was.

(b) Socioeconomic status $\to$ hormone use, socioeconomic status $\to$
heart disease, with or without an arrow from hormone use to heart
disease.

(c) The 2008 comparison. The doctor's decision is whether to start,
and that comparison follows women from the point at which they started
or did not.
:::

### Coding

Open a fresh R script. You will need the tidyverse.

#### A. Prediction and intervention

```{r coding_a_setup}
n <- 10000
# program 1: X causes Y
X1 <- rnorm(n); Y1 <- 2 * X1 + rnorm(n)
# program 2: Z causes both
Z2 <- rnorm(n); X2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n); Y2 <- Z2 + rnorm(n)
# program 3: X causes Y through M
X3 <- sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); M3 <- X3 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n); Y3 <- 0.5 * M3 + rnorm(n)
```

1. Write down the slope of $Y$ on $X$ you expect in each program. Then
   fit `lm` and compare.
2. For each program, intervene: set $X$ to 1 for everyone and run the
   statements after the one for $X$ again, then the same with $X$ set
   to 0. Compute the difference in the means of $Y$.
3. In program 2, fit `lm(Y2 ~ X2 + Z2)`. In program 3, fit
   `lm(Y3 ~ X3 + M3)`. Compare the coefficients on $X$ with your
   answers to 2.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
In each program, which statements after the one for $X$ use $X$, directly or through a variable computed from it? Those are the ones whose values change when you set $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r coding_a_solution}
slopes <- c(coef(lm(Y1 ~ X1))[2], coef(lm(Y2 ~ X2))[2], coef(lm(Y3 ~ X3))[2])
do1 <- c(mean(2 * 1 + rnorm(n)),                    # X set to 1, later statements re-run
         mean(Z2 + rnorm(n)),
         mean(0.5 * (1 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n)) + rnorm(n)))
do0 <- c(mean(2 * 0 + rnorm(n)),                    # X set to 0
         mean(Z2 + rnorm(n)),
         mean(0.5 * (0 + sqrt(2) * rnorm(n)) + rnorm(n)))
round(rbind(slope = slopes, effect = do1 - do0), 2)
round(coef(lm(Y2 ~ X2 + Z2))[2], 2)    # program 2, adjusting for Z
round(coef(lm(Y3 ~ X3 + M3))[2], 2)    # program 3, adjusting for M
```
The slopes are about 2, 0.5 and 0.5. The effects are about 2, 0 and
0.5. In programs 2 and 3, $X$ and $Y$ have the same joint distribution
(jointly normal, with means 0, variances 2 and 2 and covariance 1), so $X$ predicts
$Y$ equally well in both, and intervening on $X$ changes $Y$ only in
program 3. Adjusting for $Z$ in program 2 gives a coefficient near 0,
the effect. Adjusting for $M$ in program 3 also gives a coefficient
near 0. That is the direct effect, zero here because $X$ reaches $Y$
only through the mediator $M$; the total effect is 0.5.
:::

#### B. Adjustment on data

```{r coding_b_setup}
cells <- data.frame(Z = c(1, 1, 0, 0), X = c(1, 0, 1, 0),
                    n = c(400, 100, 100, 400), passed = c(320, 70, 50, 120))
students <- bind_rows(
  cells |> mutate(Y = 1, count = passed),
  cells |> mutate(Y = 0, count = n - passed)
) |>
  select(Z, X, Y, count) |>
  tidyr::uncount(count)
nrow(students)
```

1. Compute the pass rates of users and non-users from `students`, and
   their difference.
2. Compute the adjusted difference: the difference in pass rates within
   each value of $Z$, averaged with weights $P(Z = z)$.
3. A randomized version: give each of 1,000 students the app with
   probability 0.5, whatever their $Z$, and draw whether they pass from
   the table's rates. Compute the difference in pass rates. Repeat 200
   times. What is the average difference, and how much does it vary?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For 2: `students |> group_by(Z) |> summarize(...)` gives one row for each value of $Z$; compute the difference in pass rates and the share of students in each row there.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r coding_b_solution}
students |> group_by(X) |> summarize(rate = mean(Y))

rows <- students |>
  group_by(Z) |>
  summarize(diff = mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0]),
            share = n() / nrow(students))
sum(rows$diff * rows$share)

rate <- function(z, x) {
  ifelse(z == 1, ifelse(x == 1, 0.8, 0.7), ifelse(x == 1, 0.5, 0.3))
}
one_trial <- function() {
  Z <- rep(c(1, 0), each = 500)
  X <- rbinom(1000, 1, 0.5)
  Y <- rbinom(1000, 1, rate(Z, X))
  mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])
}
trials <- replicate(200, one_trial())
c(mean = mean(trials), sd = sd(trials))
```
1. 0.74 and 0.38, a difference of 0.36.

2. 0.15.

3. The average is close to 0.15, and the differences vary from trial to
trial with a standard deviation of about 0.03. Randomization removes
the bias without any model of $Z$, and the price is that a single trial
can miss by a few points.
:::

#### C. Intervening in a program

The job center from the lecture, as a program. As in the lecture,
everyone referred attends and nobody else does. Each line generates one
variable from the ones above it.

```{r course_starter, eval=FALSE}
n <- 10000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                        # worked last year
X <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.8, 0.2))   # attended the course
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X + 0.3 * Z)    # in work six months later
mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])             # attenders against the others
```

1. Run it. Compare the difference with the lecture's first job-center table (64% against 36%).
2. Compute the adjusted difference: the difference between attenders
   and non-attenders within $Z = 1$ and within $Z = 0$, averaged with
   weights `mean(Z == 1)` and `mean(Z == 0)`.
3. Intervene. Replace the line for `X` by `X <- rep(1, n)`, run the
   line for `Y` again, and record `mean(Y)`. Do the same with
   `X <- rep(0, n)`. Compare the difference with your answer to 2.
4. The center changes its referrals to 0.95 for $Z = 1$ and 0.05 for
   $Z = 0$. Before you run anything, write down what you expect for the
   differences in 1 and in 3. Then run it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For step 3, replace the line for `X` and leave the line for `Z` alone. Then run the line for `Y` again, so that it uses the new `X`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{r course_solution}
set.seed(313)    # the sheet's seed, so this output does not depend on the chunks above it
n <- 10000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
X <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.8, 0.2))
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X + 0.3 * Z)
observed <- mean(Y[X == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0])
d1 <- mean(Y[X == 1 & Z == 1]) - mean(Y[X == 0 & Z == 1])   # within Z = 1
d0 <- mean(Y[X == 1 & Z == 0]) - mean(Y[X == 0 & Z == 0])   # within Z = 0
adjusted <- d1 * mean(Z == 1) + d0 * mean(Z == 0)
Y1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * 1 + 0.3 * Z)    # everyone attends
Y0 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * 0 + 0.3 * Z)    # nobody attends
c(observed = observed, adjusted = adjusted, intervened = mean(Y1) - mean(Y0))

X95 <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(Z == 1, 0.95, 0.05))
Y95 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.1 * X95 + 0.3 * Z)
mean(Y95[X95 == 1]) - mean(Y95[X95 == 0])      # observed, new referrals
```
1. About $0.28$, the table's $0.64 - 0.36$.

2. About $0.10$.

3. About $0.10$: intervening deletes the arrow $Z \to X$, and the
adjusted difference estimates the same quantity.

4. The observed difference grows to about
$(0.95 \times 0.7 + 0.05 \times 0.4) - (0.05 \times 0.6 + 0.95 \times 0.3) = 0.685 - 0.315 = 0.37$.
The effect of the course stays at $0.10$: the referral policy changes
who attends, not what the course does. Each run differs from these
numbers by a few hundredths.
:::
